newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Europe's IT/telecoms market to grow 7.1 pct in '97.
newsitem.headline: Europe's IT/telecoms market to grow 7.1 pct in '97.

text.p: Western Europe's information and communications technologies (ICT) market is expected to grow by 7.1 percent in 1997, continuing an upturn that began in 1993, a study published by an industry group on Tuesday showed.

However, officials who presented the figures at a news conference noted that growth in 1996, 7.2 percent, was lower than expected and warned that Europe's market lagged behind those of the United States and some Asian countries.
"Europe is really risking to lose ground," said Bruno Lamborghini, chairman of the European Information Technology Observatory (EITO), which published the annual report.
"Even a growth rate of seven percent is not good enough," agreed Magnus Lemmel, deputy director general of the European Commission's industry department.
He said European companies were still acting too conservatively in investing in the new technologies.
The EITO forecast that Western Europe's ICT sector, which represented 34 percent of the global market, would grow to a value of 338 billion Ecus ($382 billion) in 1997.

The information technology market, representing 47 percent of the sector, will grow 6.8 percent, while the telecoms sector will grow 7.3 percent, it said. That compares with growth of 6.5 percent and 7.9 percent respectively in 1996.

EITO, an industry-funded research group based in Frankfurt, forecast last year that the ICT market would grow 8.5 percent in 1996. But Lamborghini, also president of the computer industry group Eurobit, said growth had been hindered by Europe's general economic slowdown in the first half of the year.
The new figures, based on revenues paid to primary vendors, are down from 1995, when Europe's ICT market grew 8.1 percent. But they are still up from 1993, when it grew only 3.7 percent.
EITO said market growth in 1998 would be roughly the same as this year.

Europe is lagging behind world growth of 9.5 percent in 1996 and an expected 8.8 percent in 1997, it said. The U.S. market is expected to grow 9.2 percent this year, while some countries in Latin America, Asia and Africa will see growth rates of between 10 percent and 12 percent, it added.

Western Europe's strongest markets are mobile telephone services, where growth of 18 percent is expected this year; cable television, 26 percent; switched data and leased line services, 18.5 percent; and software, 9.5 percent.
Lamborghini said Europeans spent 820 Ecus ($935) per head for ITC products and services in 1996, compared with more than 1,400 Ecus ($1,600) in the United States.

A study carried out recently for the EU by consultants Booz-Allen and Hamilton warned that Europe's ICT industries were falling behind competitors in the United States and Japan, citing a "fragmentation" of policies, standards and infrastructure elements.

Lemmel said the European Commission was pursuing several avenues to help boost Europe's competitiveness, including liberalising telecoms markets, promoting technical standards and electronic commerce, cooperating globally on issues such as intellectual property and fostering research.
